summary: Design Y is the stronger overall proposal: it reduces cognitive and movement load for first-time 5–6-year-olds while preserving the birthday-dinosaur discovery loop. Design X is more spatially specified and offers a more vivid egg-hatching payoff.

differences.design_x: Design X uses five ordered checkpoints, two eggs, two hazards, a return-to-last-point penalty, then a portal in three minutes.
differences.design_y: Design Y uses four ordered checkpoints, one hazard, and a simple egg-to-nest objective before its portal.
differences.evidence: In the options step, Design X specifies five points and two mud puddles; Design Y specifies four points and one puddle. Both prototype flows target three minutes.

differences.design_x: Design X specifies a 1.2 m clear walking corridor and keeps all checkpoints and hazards at least 0.6 m from the edge.
differences.design_y: Design Y keeps props 0.6 m from the playable edge only “where possible” and calls the hazard section a “narrow route,” despite also requesting a comfortable bypass.
differences.evidence: Final build-plan layout briefs for Design X and Design Y.

differences.design_x: Design X asks children to avoid two mud hazards while completing more stops.
differences.design_y: Design Y asks them to avoid only one mud hazard and explicitly keeps dinosaurs static beside the route.
differences.evidence: Prototype-plan decisions/storyboards and final build-plan rules in both designs.

differences.design_x: Design X culminates in two eggs hatching in front of a mother dinosaur, with sparkles, then a cake and party portal.
differences.design_y: Design Y returns an egg to a nest, then opens a cake portal; its dinosaurs are static scene props.
differences.evidence: Design X prototype storyboard, “Surprise hatching”; Design Y prototype storyboard, “Return egg to nest,” and final layout brief.

differences.design_x: Design X says it is untimed, but its prototype decisions promise a “time bonus”; it also says each point is worth 100 while separately saying the game can end at 300 plus bonus.
differences.design_y: Design Y also claims a time bonus while its HUD, rules, and game object say there is no timer.
differences.evidence: Prototype-plan scoring decisions in Design X and Design Y; both final game objects set timeLimit to null.

differences.design_x: Design X angles the hatching, cake, second hazard, and portal toward the sofa, giving spectators multiple readable moments.
differences.design_y: Design Y angles the mud dodge and cake portal toward the sofa and explicitly avoids ranking children.
differences.evidence: Final build-plan layout briefs and spectator plans.

why: Design Y better matches a short, first-VR birthday turn for preschoolers. Its main advantage is restraint: fewer required stops and hazards reduce confusion and accidental movement. Design X’s explicit corridor dimensions and stronger hatching climax are worth borrowing.
x_weaknesses: Too many sequential tasks and hazards for a three-minute first-time preschool experience.
Untimed play conflicts with a stated time bonus.
Score totals are not clearly reconciled.
y_weaknesses: Its physical-route dimensions are less firm than Design X’s.
“Narrow route” conflicts with its safety goal.
An untimed game still includes a time bonus.
improvements: Use Design Y’s four-stop, one-hazard structure with Design X’s mandatory 1.2 m corridor and 0.6 m edge clearance.
Replace all time bonuses with a fixed completion celebration or cooperative sticker reward.
Add Design X’s gentle egg-hatching moment at Design Y’s nest as the climax.
